title: Jackdaw field consent is correct for UK climate targets and the economy, Wood Mackenzie analysis shows
gist: The UK granted fresh consent on 21 October 2026 for the Shell/Equinor-owned Jackdaw gas/condensate field, and Wood Mackenzie argues approval was right: blocking it would have meant more emissions-intensive US LNG imports (+3.5 MtCO2e), forgone tax receipts of about GBP1.5 billion and a likely loss of over GBP20 billion of future UKCS investment.

insights.claim: The UK government and OPRED granted fresh consent for the Jackdaw gas/condensate field on 21 October 2026, with first gas possible within weeks.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
entities: Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero
insights.so_what: Removes a key North Sea permitting overhang and brings near-term UK gas supply online.
insights.locator: The UK government has granted fresh consent

insights.claim: The new Jackdaw consent ends a process dating to January 2025, when a judicial review suspended the original 2022 consent because scope 3 emissions had not been fully considered.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Scope 3 judicial-review risk is the template for delays to other UK North Sea projects.
insights.locator: The decision ends a process dating back to January 2025

insights.claim: The regulator accepted Adura's submission that Jackdaw's climate impact is not significant and will not materially affect UK climate commitments.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Signals how regulators may treat scope 3 assessments for pending fields such as Rosebank and Cambo.

insights.claim: Jackdaw is the biggest pre-production asset on the UKCS after Rosebank and Cambo, so its consent is a bellwether for those larger developments.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Watch Rosebank and Cambo decisions for confirmation of the consent regime's direction.
insights.locator: Jackdaw is a 68 mmboe gas/condensate field

insights.claim: Jackdaw is a 68 mmboe gas/condensate field 225 km east of Aberdeen, 100% owned by Adura, a 50/50 joint venture of Shell UK and Equinor UK, with GBP1.2 billion invested to date.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Sunk capital of GBP1.2 billion means consent unlocks returns on already-spent money for Shell and Equinor.
insights.locator: Jackdaw is a 68 mmboe gas/condensate field

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie forecasts Jackdaw gas production in 2027 will average 140 million cubic feet per day, about 6% of UKCS gas supply.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A 6% share is material to UK domestic supply and import dependence.

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie estimates Jackdaw will generate GBP430 million of post-tax cash flow for Adura in 2027 alone.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Rapid cash payback for Shell and Equinor partners once first gas starts.
insights.locator: For Adura, we estimate Jackdaw will generate

insights.claim: Higher prices lift the Jackdaw project IRR from 9% to over 14%, according to Wood Mackenzie.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Shows how sensitive marginal North Sea projects are to the current gas price spike.
insights.locator: For Adura, we estimate Jackdaw will generate

insights.claim: Jackdaw will account for 11% of Adura's net production over the project's lifetime.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Gauges the field's weight within the Shell/Equinor JV portfolio.
insights.locator: The stakes extended well beyond a single field

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie's P50 estimate puts Jackdaw's total greenhouse gas emissions over its nine-year life at 24 MtCO2e, equal to 1.8% of remaining UKCS emissions.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Quantifies the small emissions footprint that underpinned the consent argument.
insights.locator: Wood Mackenzie's P50 estimate puts total greenhouse gas emissions

insights.claim: UK gas demand is more than double UKCS supply and the UK will remain a net gas importer in all scenarios including net zero, so domestic gas displaces imports rather than adding to total supply.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Import dependence supports the political case for sustaining domestic production.
insights.locator: The emissions case rests on what domestic production displaces

insights.claim: Replacing Jackdaw's output with equivalent US LNG would have caused a net increase of 3.5 MtCO2e in scope 1 and 2 emissions.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Central argument that blocking domestic gas can raise net emissions; expect it reused in other UK consent cases.
insights.quote: Blocking Jackdaw would require the UK to import more emissions-intensive LNG to meet UK gas demand.

insights.claim: The UK Climate Change Committee says meeting carbon budgets requires cutting fossil fuel demand through EV, heat pump and electrification uptake, and blocking domestic gas supply would not have advanced that.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Frames demand-side policy, not supply blocking, as the lever for climate targets.
insights.locator: The UK Climate Change Committee is clear

insights.claim: NBP gas prices have climbed above 200 pence per therm, the highest since 2022, while Brent has again surged past US$100 per barrel.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Elevated UK gas and oil prices raise the stakes for supply policy and energy-cost inflation.
insights.locator: The decision arrives as energy prices have moved sharply higher

insights.claim: Under Q4 2026 base price assumptions, Jackdaw could yield about GBP1.5 billion (nominal) of government tax receipts, a 69% share of remaining undiscounted pre-tax cash flow, with 80% accruing in this parliament.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: A heavy fiscal take at high prices strengthens the Treasury's incentive to back North Sea consents.
insights.quote: At current prices, Jackdaw could generate £1.5 billion in vital tax receipts for the Treasury.
insights.locator: Under our Q4 2026 base price assumptions

insights.claim: Had Jackdaw been refused, Wood Mackenzie assessed that over GBP20 billion (real terms) of future UKCS greenfield investment would very likely have been lost, along with industry confidence in the consent process.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Consent certainty is the key variable for UK upstream capital allocation and services demand.
insights.quote: over £20 billion of future greenfield UKCS investment would very likely be lost

insights.claim: Jackdaw and Rosebank together are expected to support over 800 jobs and deliver a combined 20-year gross value add of over GBP25 billion to the UK economy.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Employment and GVA figures are the political counterweight to climate objections for Rosebank.
insights.locator: Jackdaw and Rosebank together are expected

insights.claim: Wood Mackenzie's research director argues the correct way to tackle the climate crisis is to reduce demand for oil and gas, and that North Sea production should remain a vital part of the UK energy mix.
insights.speaker: Wood Mackenzie
insights.so_what: Illustrates the industry's demand-side framing used to defend continued supply.
insights.quote: The correct way to tackle the climate crisis is to reduce demand for oil and gas.
